parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **NaturaBite Foods (NF)**
> 
> NaturaBite Foods (NF) is a private limited company in country G that produces organic snack foods, including energy bars, dried fruit mixes, and nut butters. NF sells its products to supermarkets and health food stores across country G. NF has built a strong brand with the slogan 'nothing artificial, nothing hidden'.
> 
> NF currently uses flow production to manufacture its products in large quantities. The production manager believes that switching to batch production will allow NF to produce a wider range of flavours and varieties, responding to changing customer preferences. However, the Finance Director has raised concerns about the cost of reorganising the production process.
> 
> NF employs 60 workers in one factory. The Production Manager believes there is significant room to improve labour productivity without increasing headcount. Table 2.1 shows NF's financial data for 2023.
> 
> **Table 2.1: NF financial data 2023**
> 
> |   |   |
> |---|---|
> | Selling price per unit (\$) | 4.00 |
> | Variable cost per unit (\$) | 1.50 |
> | Total fixed costs (\$) | 75,000 |
> | Current annual output (units) | 40,000 |
> | Maximum capacity (units) | 55,000 |

Analyse **two** ways NF could improve its labour productivity.
parts.solution_md:
One way NF could improve labour productivity is by introducing incentives for its workers, such as performance-related pay linked to output targets **[K]**. At the moment, NF has spare capacity, producing 40,000 units against a maximum of 55,000 **[Ap]**, so there is clear room to produce more with the same 60 employees. If workers are rewarded for higher output, they may work harder and waste less time during shifts **[An]**. This could help NF get closer to its maximum capacity without hiring extra staff, which would spread its \$75,000 of fixed costs over more units and lower the average cost of each item produced **[An]**

Another way NF could improve labour productivity is by redesigning its production process to cut out wasted time and movement **[K]**, following lean production ideas. NF currently uses flow production, and its production manager is already reviewing how production works because of the idea to introduce batch production **[Ap]**. As part of this review, NF could look for delays or inefficient steps in the current flow line and remove them. This would let the existing 60 workers produce more units in the same shift length **[An]**, raising output per worker without needing to spend money on new machinery or extra staff **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the** **impacts on a business of ways NF could improve labour productivity in its production process |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the impacts on NF of improving labour productivityin its production process |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the** **impacts on NF of improving labour productivityin its production process |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of labour productivity |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative Content**
> 
> - Training and development - NF's production manager believes there is room to improve productivity without increasing headcount. Investing in targeted training for NF's 60 production workers (e.g. on machine operation, quality control or food hygiene) would help them complete tasks more efficiently and with fewer errors. A more skilled, more confident workforce is also likely to be more motivated, reducing absenteeism and labour turnover; even small efficiency gains across all 60 employees would cumulatively raise output without extra staff, lowering NF's average cost per unit, especially given NF currently has spare capacity to fill (40,000 units against a maximum of 55,000).
> - Automation of repetitive tasks - NF currently uses flow production for large-volume output; introducing automated machinery for repetitive tasks such as packaging or labelling would let the same 60 workers produce more output per shift, freeing staff to focus on higher-value tasks such as quality inspection. This raises labour productivity because output rises without an increase in headcount. However, the upfront capital cost of new machinery is high, so NF's Finance Director - already concerned about reorganisation costs - would need to weigh this against the long-term productivity gains before approving investment.
> - Financial/non-financial incentives - introducing incentives, such as performance-related pay linked to output targets or non-financial rewards, could motivate NF's workers to increase effort and reduce time wasted during shifts. As NF has spare capacity between its current output of 40,000 units and its maximum capacity of 55,000, higher motivation could help NF's existing 60 employees produce closer to this maximum without hiring more staff, spreading NF's \$75,000 of fixed costs over more units and lowering average cost per unit.
> - Redesigning production processes - reviewing and streamlining NF's flow production process to reduce wasted time, movement or waiting between stages (lean production principles) could allow workers to complete more units in the same shift length. This is particularly relevant given NF's production manager is already reviewing production methods (considering a switch to batch production for greater flexibility); removing inefficiencies in the existing flow line could raise output per worker without additional headcount or major capital spend, offering a lower-cost route to improved productivity than automation.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> For "analyse" questions worth 8 marks, always aim to cover **two** distinct points rather than writing extensively about just one. Each point should follow a clear structure: identify the way, link it to NF's situation using specific evidence from the case study, and then build a chain of reasoning explaining the consequences for the business
> 
> Many students lose application marks by writing generic answers that could apply to any business. Make sure you reference specific details about NF - such as its use of flow production, the production manager's views, or the number of employees - to demonstrate application.
> 
> For analysis, avoid simply stating an outcome. Instead, build a logical chain: explain *why* the way would work, *how* it would affect productivity, and *what* the wider implications are for NF. Using connective phrases such as "this means that…", "as a result…" and "which would lead to…" helps signal your analytical reasoning to the examiner.
> 
> Do not just list ways to improve productivity without developing them - a list of points with no reasoning will only access knowledge marks.

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process.
parts.solution_md:
One impact of increasing automation is that it can lower the business's unit costs in the long run **[K]**. For example, if a food packaging company installs automated machinery to fill and seal its products **[Ap]**, it will need fewer workers to do this job. As the machines create a higher fixed cost but a lower variable cost per unit, the more the business produces, the lower its average cost per unit becomes **[An]**. This means the business could either lower its prices to attract more customers or keep prices the same and earn a higher profit margin, improving its overall competitiveness **[An]**

Another impact is that automation is likely to reduce the number of workers the business needs **[K]**. If the food packaging company introduces machines to do tasks previously done by hand **[Ap]**, some employees may become redundant. This could save the business money on wages in the long run, but making staff redundant can be expensive in the short term due to redundancy payments, and it may lower the morale of the remaining workers **[An]**, who could worry about losing their own jobs. This may increase labour turnover or reduce motivation, which could offset some of the cost savings from automation **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the** **impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the** **impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of automation |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative Content**
> 
> - Lower unit costs - automating parts of the production process replaces variable labour costs with fixed machinery costs. For example, a food processing company that automates packaging could reduce the number of workers needed per unit produced. As output increases, the fixed cost of the machinery is spread over more units, lowering average cost per unit; this could allow the business to reduce prices or increase its profit margin, strengthening its position against competitors.
> - Increased speed and consistency of output - automated machinery can typically produce output faster and with less variation than manual labour. In a food processing company, this could mean packets are filled and sealed to a more consistent standard, reducing the amount of substandard output that has to be reworked or wasted, which could improve efficiency and protect the business's reputation for quality.
> - High initial capital cost - introducing automated machinery usually requires a large upfront investment to purchase and install the equipment. A food processing company installing an automated packaging line would need significant finance, which could increase its gearing if funded through loans or reduce cash available for other purposes, creating short-term financial pressure before any longer-term cost savings are realised.
> - Workforce reduction and redundancies - increasing automation is likely to reduce the number of workers needed for tasks machines can now perform. For a food processing company, this could mean redundancies among production line staff, involving redundancy payments and potentially damaging morale among remaining employees who fear further job losses, which could increase labour turnover or reduce motivation.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks on "analyse" questions by simply identifying an impact without developing a chain of reasoning. To reach the higher levels, make sure you explain *why* and *how* the impact occurs, linking cause to effect and then to a further consequence for the business.
> 
> Structure your answer around two impacts and develop each in depth rather than listing several impacts superficially. For example, if you choose "lower unit costs", explain how automation replaces variable labour costs with fixed machinery costs, how this affects average costs as output rises, and what this ultimately means for the business's pricing strategy or profit margins.
> 
> Always apply your answer to a realistic business context - even if the question does not name a specific business, you should create a plausible scenario (e.g. a manufacturer of standardised goods) to demonstrate application skills.
> 
> Avoid spending time discussing multiple impacts; the question asks for **one**, so depth of analysis on a single point is rewarded far more than breadth.

parts.problem_md: Discuss the view that it is more important for a manufacturer of bicycles to be effective than it is to be efficient.
parts.solution_md:
One key issue is that being efficient does not guarantee success if a bicycle manufacturer is not effective **[K]**. For example, if CycleWorks produces steel-framed bicycles very cheaply and quickly, this is efficient because it uses fewer resources per bike **[Ap]**. However, if most customers now want lightweight electric bikes because of rising fuel costs and environmental concerns, CycleWorks would be efficient but ineffective, because it is not meeting what customers actually want **[An]**. This could mean CycleWorks produces bicycles that do not sell, wasting the benefit of its low production costs and losing revenue to competitors offering more relevant products **[An]**

However, efficiency is still important because it supports CycleWorks' long-term profitability **[K]**. If CycleWorks uses technology such as computer-aided design and manufacture (CAD/CAM), it may be able to produce a wider range of bicycle designs, such as electric or folding bikes **[Ap]**, while still keeping unit costs relatively low **[An]**. This shows efficiency and effectiveness do not always conflict, and being efficient can actually help CycleWorks stay competitively priced **[An]**. Without reasonable efficiency, CycleWorks may struggle to fund the research and innovation needed to remain effective in a fast-changing market, so efficiency also indirectly supports effectiveness over time **[An]**

Overall, I think effectiveness is more important than efficiency for a bicycle manufacturer like CycleWorks **[E]**, at least in the short to medium term. The bicycle market changes quickly, with growing demand for electric and lifestyle bikes **[Ap]**, so if CycleWorks fails to meet these changing customer needs, efficient production of the wrong product will not generate sales. However, this does not mean efficiency does not matter **[E]**. CycleWorks still needs to control costs to remain profitable and to fund the innovation that keeps it effective in future **[Ap]**. A truly successful bicycle manufacturer needs a balance of both, but when trends are changing rapidly, correctly identifying and meeting customer demand should take priority over minimising costs **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **4** | - Shows understanding of two implications in context |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one implication in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two implications |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one implication |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two implications in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one implication in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two implications |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one implication |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Effectiveness means "doing the right thing" - achieving objectives such as meeting customer needs, which can lead to greater market share, sales, revenue and profit.
> - Efficiency means "doing the thing right" - converting inputs into outputs at the lowest possible cost, linked to productivity and cost-effective production.
> - Being efficient without being effective risks producing bicycles that do not sell, wasting the benefit of low production costs; unsold stock and lost sales can outweigh any savings made through efficient production.
> - Because bicycle design trends and customer tastes change quickly (e.g. growth in e-bikes and lifestyle cycling), the production process needs to be innovative and flexible - a manufacturer that prioritises efficiency over flexibility may be slow to respond to these changes, losing market share to more responsive rivals.
> - Efficiency can come at the expense of effectiveness if cost-cutting leads to a narrower product range that fails to meet the needs of different customer segments.
> - However, efficiency also supports profitability and can drive sustainable growth - cost control gives a manufacturer the funds and competitive pricing needed to invest in the innovation that keeps it effective over time, so the two are not always in conflict.
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - A manufacturer needs to be both efficient and effective - producing what customers want at a loss, or producing cheaply what customers don't want, are both unsustainable in the long run.
> - The balance between efficiency and effectiveness may shift at different stages of the product life cycle - effectiveness may matter more during periods of fast-changing trends (e.g. the growth stage of e-bikes), while efficiency may become more important once a design matures and competition increases on price.
> - A judgement should weigh which matters more specifically for a bicycle manufacturer given how quickly trends in this market change, reaching a supported conclusion.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md: Define the term ‘productivity’.
parts.solution_md:

Kwom estimates that this new venture would require additional finance of \$350000. parts.solution_md:
One advantage of job production for HH is that it allows Hannah and Kwom to make unique bags for each customer **[K]**. This fits with HH's brand as a niche, well known producer of luxury handbags. Because each bag is different, customers may be willing to pay higher prices for something no one else has **[An]**, which could help explain why HH already earns a high gross profit margin of around 40% **[An]**

One disadvantage of job production is that it can take a long time to make each bag **[K]. **This slow production speed is fine for HH's current niche market, where customers expect a bespoke product  **[Ap]**. However, Hannah and Kwom are now planning to expand into batch-produced bags sold online, in a market with 15 large competitors where bags must be priced competitively **[An]**. ‘In a large computer manufacturing business, the operations department is more important for achieving success than the marketing department.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
The operations department is responsible for turning inputs, such as materials and components, into finished computers that meet the standards customers expect. This includes choosing the best production method, selecting reliable suppliers, and checking the quality of the final product **[K]**. If TechCore's operations department works efficiently, computers will be made to a high standard, at a reasonable cost, and delivered on time. This is important because even if customers want to buy TechCore's computers, poor quality or late production could damage TechCore's reputation **[Ap] **and cause it to lose customers to competitors, no matter how good its marketing has been **[An]** However, the marketing department is also essential, because it identifies exactly what customers want before operations even begins production **[K]**. Marketing research tells TechCore what specifications, features **[Ap]** and price customers expect from a new computer. Without this information, operations could produce computers that nobody wants to buy, wasting resources on unsold stock. Marketing also builds TechCore's brand and communicates why customers should choose TechCore over competitors, which drives the sales that operations then has to fulfil **[An]** This shows that the two departments are closely interdependent **[K]**, and one cannot succeed without the other. If marketing promises features or delivery times that operations cannot actually achieve, customers will be left disappointed regardless of which department is considered more important. In a large business like TechCore, close communication between the two departments is essential to avoid this happening **[An]** It could also be argued that neither operations nor marketing is the most important department in a computer manufacturing business, because the technology industry changes so quickly. Without continuous investment in research and development, TechCore's products could quickly become outdated compared to competitors **[Ap]**, no matter how efficient its operations are or how well its marketing team performs **[An]**. This may help Ralph attract customers back to his shop even though his prices might be higher **[An]**

Making each frame individually, instead of in a batch, takes more time and materials per item, so each frame will cost Ralph more to produce **[An]**. > - Meets customer's specific needs / unique product - Ralph's frames can be made in any size and from a variety of materials chosen by the customer, making each frame unique. > - Greater job satisfaction - job production can be more varied and challenging than repetitive batch production. As Ralph currently prints similar batches of photographs, moving to making unique, individually designed frames could make his work more rewarding, keeping him motivated to grow the business despite tough competition

parts.problem_md: Analyse the advantages to a business of using mass customisation.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage is that mass customisation helps a business meet the different needs of its customers **[K]**. For example, a trainers company could let customers choose the colour or add their initials to a mostly standard shoe design **[Ap]**. This means customers feel like they are getting a personalised product, even though most of the production process is the same as normal mass production **[An]**. This is likely to increase customer satisfaction and encourage repeat purchases, which can increase the business's sales and market share over time **[An]**

Another advantage is that mass customisation can keep costs relatively low compared with fully bespoke production **[K]**. This is because most of the materials and components used, like the base of the trainer **[Ap]**, are still the same across all versions of the product. This means the business can still benefit from bulk-buying discounts on these shared parts, even though the finished product looks different for each customer **[An]**. As a result, the business can offer variety and charge a slightly higher price without losing the cost advantages of mass production, which should protect its profit margins **[An]**

parts.solution_md:
One important issue is the financial risk of the investment **[K]**. Table 2.1 shows the total cost of the new factory would be \$265,000 (land, machinery and training). DC is profitable but has no retained earnings **[Ap]**, which means it has no spare cash of its own to fund this. DC would need to borrow the money or find external investment, which creates risk because the co-op is owned by farmers rather than shareholders who might expect a quicker return **[An]**. If sales of cocoa butter are lower than expected, DC could struggle to repay this debt, which could reduce the short-term income of the 500 farming families who depend on DC **[Ap]** **[An]**

A second important issue is DC's workforce problem. Zara's workforce plan shows that young people do not want to work on the farms because of a lack of training, mostly manual work, and little control over earnings **[Ap]**. The new factory would include \$15,000 of training and would involve more capital-intensive, machine-based work rather than fully manual farming. This directly addresses two of the three concerns young people have, which could help DC attract and keep younger workers in the future **[Ap]** **[An]**. Without this change, DC risks a shortage of workers as older farmers retire, which would threaten its long-term supply of raw cocoa beans **[Ap]** **[An]**

Overall, I think DC should go ahead with the new factory **[E]**. The financial risk is real, since DC has no retained earnings and \$265,000 is a large sum for a farming co-operative to borrow **[Ap]**. However, DC's own research shows that its current way of working is not sustainable, because young people are turning away from farm work. The factory tackles this problem directly through training and less manual work **[E]**, while also processing beans into a higher-margin product, since cocoa butter sells for \$10,000 per tonne against variable costs of \$5,000 per tonne. This extra profit could help DC repay any borrowing and support its triple bottom line objective **[Ap]** by securing jobs for the community's future, so the long-term benefits are likely to outweigh the short-term financial risk **[E]**

They work closely with each customer, like Ikram did with Lydia, choosing fabric and colour to make a unique dress **[Ap]**. If DC moves to batch production, machinery will be used to make the trousers instead of relying on the designers' individual skills. This means employees' skills may not be needed as much, so they could feel their expertise is being wasted **[An]**. This could lower motivation and job satisfaction, which may cause slower work or lower quality trousers, harming DC's reputation **[An]**

Another problem is fear of change **[K]**. DC's employees are used to a stable way of working, meeting customers directly and being paid hourly rates for skilled work **[Ap]**. Introducing batch production and new machinery is a big change, so employees may worry about losing their jobs or having to learn new skills quickly **[An]**. If Khaleal does not communicate clearly with staff about why the change is happening and how it will affect them, employees may resist the new system. This could cause delays in setting up batch production and could lower morale across DC as a whole **[An]**

parts.problem_md: Explain the difference between efficiency and effectiveness in business operations.
parts.solution_md:
Efficiency means producing output using the minimum amount of inputs — in other words, getting the most from the resources available and keeping unit costs low. Effectiveness means achieving the business's objectives and meeting the needs of customers — producing the right product or service, not just producing it cheaply. A business can be efficient without being effective: for example, a manufacturer might produce large quantities of a product at very low cost, but if customers do not want that product, the business will not meet its sales targets or generate profit. True business success requires both — producing the right output in the most cost-effective way possible

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Efficiency is about producing the maximum output from a given level of inputs - often described as 'doing things right'; it focuses on minimising waste and reducing cost per unit
> - Effectiveness is about achieving the right business objectives and meeting customer needs - often described as 'doing the right things'; it focuses on whether the business is producing what customers actually want
> - The key difference: efficiency is about HOW a business produces its output; effectiveness is about WHETHER that output is the right one
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A business can be highly efficient without being effective - for example, a factory might produce thousands of units at very low cost per unit (high efficiency), but if those units do not meet customer needs or market demand, the business will still fail to achieve its objectives; this shows that efficiency alone is not enough - the business also needs to ensure it is producing the right goods or services for its target market
> - The relationship between efficiency and effectiveness depends on the market a business operates in; a business competing in a volume, low-cost market segment needs both - it must produce efficiently to keep costs down, and effectively to meet the basic needs of price-sensitive customers; however, a business in an exclusive designer market may accept lower efficiency (higher cost per unit) as long as it is highly effective at meeting the expectations of quality-conscious customers
> 
> Accept any other valid response
